418.t: Blending in a section and the role of the lead
418.s: Sections blend if players balance volume; only the lead should stand out slightly.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Some guys blow their horn and make it too loud for this other horn, you know. And they're all supposed to blend together and make it all come out with the same volume. That's what you want. The right volume of each instrument so that each can be heard. Not that you overshadow this other instrument.

2.t: Cooperation in the band; his Chicago interviews by instrument
2.s: Russell says working together is the core of New Orleans style and describes interviewing Baby Dodds, Omer Simeon, Roy Palmer and Natty Dominique.
2.q: Or else it's the type of people that, for one thing, one of the great principles which you can't really overemphasize in New Orleans music, in the jazz, is the working together. 868.t: How a six-piece band started a tune and how choruses were shared
868.s: De De describes the band starting together, the trumpet's two-beat lead-in, keys, and trumpet resting his lip while others take choruses.
868.q: Oh no, we'd all start off together. We'd give the name of the piece quite nicely, most every man member of the band knew the number, melody anyway.

253.t: Kid Thomas's simple style and playing behind it
253.s: Ralph asks about Kid Thomas's sparse trumpet style; Hall says simple lead makes it easy to fill in.
253.q: Yeah, I imagine it's all right. I started with Thomas because Thomas is still playing the same way. Yeah, I know you played. Yeah.

409.s: Blending means staying under the lead; only the earliest trumpet section tried to be one man.
